Sup A: seidel_2018_detailed_kinetic_model · Kinetic modeling of methanol synthesis from renewable resources (Detailed kinetic model)
The detailed kinetic model describes methanol synthesis from hydrogen, carbon monoxide, and carbon dioxide over a commercial copper/zinc oxide/alumina catalyst. It predicts the rates of CO hydrogenation, CO₂ hydrogenation, and the reverse water-gas shift reaction from gas partial pressures and temperature. It uses a Langmuir–Hinshelwood framework built from elementary surface steps, with fast steps treated as quasi-equilibrated. The detailed kinetic formulation is steady-state and algebraic, rather than a dynamic model with evolving states. Its parameters were fitted to 140 steady-state experiments in a differential Micro-Berty reactor and its predictions were compared with those measurements; dynamic switching experiments in the paper were used for a separate model extension. The authors present the kinetics as a basis for modelling methanol reactors handling changing feed compositions, including for chemical energy storage.

Sup B: vandenbussche_1996 · A Steady-State Kinetic Model for Methanol Synthesis and the Water Gas Shift Reaction on a Commercial Cu/ZnO/ $ Al_{2}O_{3} $ Catalyst
The model describes methanol synthesis and the reverse water-gas-shift reaction over a commercial Cu/ZnO/Al₂O₃ catalyst. It predicts the rates of both reactions and, when coupled to reactor material balances, gas conversions and concentration profiles. The kinetic equations are derived from a surface reaction scheme, with the two reactions coupled through a shared surface oxygen intermediate. The authors estimated parameters from integral bench-reactor experiments and used the fitted model to examine changes in temperature, pressure, and feed composition, including conditions outside the experimental range. They present it as a physically grounded model for predicting catalyst behavior, and make the full experimental data set available from the corresponding author.

answer.description: A and B are mechanistic steady-state kinetic models of methanol synthesis and the reverse water-gas-shift reaction over commercial Cu/ZnO/Al₂O₃ catalysts, and both address how feed composition and operating conditions affect reaction behavior. They are worth comparing as alternative descriptions of this process; A’s paper specifically compares its predictions with B. A includes explicit CO hydrogenation as well as CO₂ hydrogenation, whereas B couples methanol synthesis and reverse water-gas shift through a shared surface oxygen intermediate. A was fitted to differential Micro-Berty reactor experiments using partial pressures, while B was fitted to integral bench-reactor conversions and considered fugacities. A’s paper reports that B could not reproduce its pure-CO experiments and had larger deviations on other experiments.
